html:
The main northern gate of Babylon, built about 575 BCE by Nebuchadnezzar II of the Neo-Babylonian Empire and dedicated to the goddess Ishtar. Its walls were faced with bricks glazed deep blue and set with rows of bulls and dragons in yellow and brown.

The dragon was the mušḫuššu, beast of the city god Marduk; the bulls belonged to the storm god Adad. The gate opened onto the Processional Way, lined with glazed lions, along which the statues of the gods were carried during the New Year festival. Nebuchadnezzar built it as part of a vast rebuilding that made Babylon one of the great cities of the ancient world, the same king who destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BCE.

German archaeologists under Robert Koldewey dug it out between 1902 and 1914. The front part of the gate was rebuilt from the original bricks in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin, where it still stands. Smaller pieces are in museums around the world, and a replica stands at the site in Iraq.
